caption:
Oregon and Virginia sued SpaceX on November 23 over sexual deepfakes made with Grok, including images of children.
The states say SpaceX promoted Grok's "spicy mode" while telling users it had zero tolerance for this content.
They want court orders, civil penalties and the profits back. SpaceX did not immediately comment.

paragraphs.text: Oregon and Virginia sued SpaceX on Monday, November 23, 2026, over sexualized images created with Grok, the AI chatbot available to users of X. Virginia Attorney General Jay Jones and Oregon Attorney General Dan Rayfield filed separate but coordinated cases, according to The Record. AP and Reuters reported that the two states are the first to sue over Grok, after several states opened investigations in recent months.

The Record reported that the suits name SpaceX, its social platform X and SpaceX Super Intelligence, the company formerly known as xAI, which makes Grok. AP and Reuters described X as a SpaceX subsidiary and said the cases were filed in state courts under each state's consumer protection laws.

At the center of both cases is Grok's "spicy mode," a feature that the states say let users take a photo of a person and produce a nude or sexual image or video. The complaints argue that SpaceX promoted the feature and its chatbot's "rebellious streak" while assuring the public that it had a zero tolerance policy for such material, which the states call false.

Virginia's complaint says executives saw the content as a way to grow market share. Jones said the company removed industry standard safeguards to push Grok to tens of millions of new users, and that the weak safeguards "were not a failure but a feature," according to both reports.

According to The Record, the suits say Grok's user base surged in December 2025 after people discovered they could create nude images from a single photo. They cite a study by the Center for Countering Digital Hate that found Grok created and posted about 3 million sexualized images on X over eight days starting in late December 2025, about 23,000 of which depicted children. AP and Reuters reported the child figure as more than 20,000. The Record added that almost 30 percent of the child images flagged by the group remained on X for a week or longer.

The states also say the problem continues. Virginia investigators found Grok's moderation inconsistent and said the chatbot advised users on how to avoid moderation triggers. AP and Reuters reported that Grok began telling users in January that image features were limited to paying subscribers, which the suit says did not stop the images and let the company profit from them.
What the states want and how SpaceX responded

The states are asking for injunctions to stop the practices, civil penalties, legal costs and the return of illegal profits, The Record reported. AP and Reuters said they also seek damages. SpaceX did not immediately respond to requests for comment. X's safety team posted a statement on Monday that did not directly address the lawsuits, saying X blocks sexualized or nude prompts and works with law enforcement.

The cases add to existing pressure on the company. AP and Reuters reported that SpaceX already faces more than a dozen individual lawsuits over Grok images, and The Record noted that California Attorney General Rob Bonta announced an investigation into xAI in January over similar alleged conduct.

The suits rely on consumer protection law rather than new AI rules, arguing that the gap between the company's safety promises and what the product did amounted to deception. If that approach holds up in court, other states could use the same laws against AI image tools without waiting for new legislation.
Watch whether other states that opened Grok investigations file their own suits, and whether a court orders limits on Grok's image features while the cases proceed.
